PART 1

Organization of Ecosystems

Levels of Organization · Biotic and Abiotic Factors · Biomes · Habitats · Niches

Lesson 1 · Levels of Ecological Organization · Lesson 2 · Habitats and Niches

LESSON 1: LEVELS OF ECOLOGICAL ORGANIZATION

Ecology is the study of how organisms interact with each other and with their environment. Ecologists study life at many different scales, from a single brook trout in a Pennsylvania stream to the entire planet.

1.1 From Organism to Biosphere

Ecologists organize the living world into levels. Each level includes everything in the level below it, plus something more.

  • Organism — one individual living thing, such as one brook trout.
  • Population — all the members of one species living in the same area at the same time, such as all the brook trout in one stream.
  • Community — all the populations of different species living and interacting in an area: the trout, crayfish, mayflies, algae, and streamside plants.
  • Ecosystem — the community plus the nonliving parts of its environment, such as water, rocks, sunlight, and temperature.
  • Biome — a large region of Earth with a similar climate and similar kinds of communities, such as the temperate deciduous forest that covers most of Pennsylvania.
  • Biosphere — every part of Earth where life exists, from the deep ocean to the upper atmosphere.
VOCABULARY
Ecology — the study of interactions among organisms and between organisms and their environment.
Organism — one individual living thing.
Population — all the members of one species living in the same area at the same time.
Community — all the populations of different species that live and interact in an area.
VOCABULARY
Ecosystem — a community plus the nonliving parts of its environment.
Biome — a large region with a similar climate and similar kinds of communities.
Biosphere — all the parts of Earth where life exists.
QUICK CHECK
A biologist counts every eastern hemlock tree in a one-hectare plot of forest. Which level of organization is she studying? Explain how you know.

1.2 Biotic and Abiotic Factors

Every ecosystem has living and nonliving parts. Biotic factors are the living (or once-living) parts of an ecosystem, such as plants, animals, fungi, bacteria, and dead leaves. Abiotic factors are the nonliving physical and chemical parts, such as sunlight, temperature, water, soil, oxygen, and pH.

EcosystemBiotic factorsAbiotic factors
Pennsylvania mountain streamBrook trout, mayfly nymphs, crayfish, algae, hemlock trees on the bankCold water, dissolved oxygen, current speed, rocks, shade
Farm fieldCorn, earthworms, deer, soil bacteria, weedsSunlight, rainfall, soil nutrients, temperature
Forest floorFungi, salamanders, ferns, fallen leavesMoisture, soil pH, shade, humidity

Biotic and abiotic factors constantly affect each other. Cold, oxygen-rich water lets brook trout survive. In turn, the hemlock trees along the bank shade the stream and keep the water cold. If the trees are cut down, the water warms, holds less oxygen, and the trout may disappear.

VOCABULARY
Biotic factor — a living or once-living part of an ecosystem.
Abiotic factor — a nonliving physical or chemical part of an ecosystem.

1.3 Biomes

The type of biome found in a place depends mostly on its climate, the average temperature and precipitation over many years. Climate determines which plants can grow, and the plants determine which animals can live there.

BiomeClimateTypical organisms
TundraVery cold; little precipitation; frozen soil (permafrost)Mosses, lichens, caribou, arctic fox
Taiga (boreal forest)Long, cold winters; moderate precipitationSpruce, fir, moose, lynx
Temperate deciduous forestFour seasons; plenty of rainOak, maple, white-tailed deer, black bear
GrasslandHot summers, cold winters; moderate rainGrasses, bison, prairie dogs
DesertVery dry; hot days, cool nightsCacti, lizards, kangaroo rats
Tropical rain forestWarm all year; very heavy rainVines, orchids, monkeys, the most species of any biome
VOCABULARY
Climate — the average temperature and precipitation of an area over many years.
QUICK CHECK
Two places have the same average temperature. One gets 25 cm of rain a year and the other gets 150 cm. Predict which biome each place might be and explain your reasoning.

LESSON 2: HABITATS AND NICHES

A white-tailed deer and a pileated woodpecker can live in the same Pennsylvania forest and still lead very different lives. Ecologists describe these differences using two ideas: habitat and niche.

2.1 Habitat

An organism's habitat is the place where it lives: the area that provides the food, water, shelter, and other conditions it needs. A habitat is like an organism's address. The habitat of a brook trout is a cold, clear, well-oxygenated stream.

2.2 Niche

An organism's niche is its role in the ecosystem: everything about how it lives and how it uses its habitat. If the habitat is the address, the niche is the job. A niche includes:

  • what the organism eats and what eats it
  • where and when it feeds (treetops or ground, day or night)
  • how and when it reproduces
  • the range of abiotic conditions, such as temperature and pH, in which it can survive

Every species can survive only within a certain range of tolerance for each abiotic factor. Brook trout, for example, do best in water below about 20 °C. Outside its range of tolerance, an organism becomes stressed, stops reproducing, or dies.

VOCABULARY
Habitat — the place where an organism lives and gets what it needs to survive.
Niche — an organism's role in its ecosystem, including what it eats, where and when it feeds, and the conditions it can tolerate.
Range of tolerance — the range of an abiotic factor, such as temperature, within which an organism can survive.

2.3 Competitive Exclusion

What happens when two species try to fill the same niche? In the 1930s, the scientist G. F. Gause grew two species of Paramecium in the same container with the same food. When grown alone, each species did well. When grown together, one species always outcompeted the other and drove it to zero.

This led to the competitive exclusion principle: two species cannot occupy exactly the same niche in the same place for very long. One will be better at using the shared resources and will eventually exclude the other.

2.4 Resource Partitioning

Similar species often avoid competitive exclusion by dividing up resources. In the 1950s, ecologist Robert MacArthur studied several species of warblers that all ate insects in the same spruce trees. He found that each species fed in a different part of the tree. This is called resource partitioning. Because each species has a slightly different niche, all of them can live in the same habitat.

VOCABULARY
Competitive exclusion principle — the idea that two species cannot occupy exactly the same niche in the same place for long.
Resource partitioning — the division of resources among similar species so that each uses them in a different way, place, or time.

2.5 Fundamental and Realized Niches

The full range of conditions and resources a species could use is its fundamental niche. Competition and predators usually keep a species from using all of it. The part it actually uses is its realized niche. For example, a barnacle species may be able to survive on an entire rocky shoreline, but a stronger competitor crowds it out of the lower rocks, so it lives only on the upper rocks.

VOCABULARY
Fundamental niche — the full range of conditions and resources a species could use.
Realized niche — the part of the fundamental niche a species actually uses because of competition and other interactions.
QUICK CHECK
Brook trout and brown trout compete for the same insects in a stream. Brown trout can tolerate warmer water than brook trout. Predict which species is more likely to remain if the stream slowly warms. Explain using the term range of tolerance.

PART 2

Interactions and Populations

Competition · Predation · Symbiosis · Population Growth · Carrying Capacity

Lesson 3 · Ecological Interactions · Lesson 4 · Population Growth and Carrying Capacity

LESSON 3: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS

No organism lives alone. Every population in a community interacts with others, competing for resources, eating or being eaten, or living in close partnership. These interactions shape the size of every population.

3.1 Competition

Competition happens when organisms need the same limited resource, such as food, water, light, space, or mates. Competition harms both competitors, because each one gets less of the resource.

  • Intraspecific competition is competition between members of the same species, such as two male deer competing for a mate.
  • Interspecific competition is competition between different species, such as maple and oak seedlings competing for sunlight on the forest floor.
VOCABULARY
Competition — an interaction in which organisms need the same limited resource.
Intraspecific competition — competition between members of the same species.
Interspecific competition — competition between members of different species.

3.2 Predation and Herbivory

In predation, one organism (the predator) kills and eats another (the prey). A red-tailed hawk catching a field mouse is predation. In herbivory, an animal eats plants or parts of plants, as when deer browse on young trees.

Prey species have adaptations that help them avoid predators, such as camouflage, warning colors, speed, spines, or toxic chemicals. Predators have adaptations for catching prey, such as sharp vision, speed, and claws.

Predator and prey populations often rise and fall in linked cycles. Fur-trading records from Canada show that when snowshoe hares become plentiful, lynx have more food and their numbers rise. More lynx eat more hares, so the hare population falls. With less food, the lynx population then falls too, and the cycle repeats.

VOCABULARY
Predation — an interaction in which one organism kills and eats another.
Herbivory — an interaction in which an animal eats plants or parts of plants.
QUICK CHECK
Look at the graph. Why does each peak in the lynx population come a few years after a peak in the hare population?

3.3 Symbiosis

Symbiosis is a close, long-term relationship between two different species. There are three main types:

TypeSpecies 1Species 2Example
Mutualism+ helped+ helpedBees get nectar from flowers; flowers get pollinated.
Commensalism+ helped0 not affectedBarnacles ride on a whale and filter food; the whale is not affected.
Parasitism+ helped (parasite)− harmed (host)A deer tick feeds on a white-tailed deer's blood.
VOCABULARY
Symbiosis — a close, long-term relationship between two different species.
Mutualism — a relationship in which both species benefit.
Commensalism — a relationship in which one species benefits and the other is not affected.
Parasitism — a relationship in which one species (the parasite) benefits and the other (the host) is harmed.

3.4 Keystone Species and Trophic Cascades

A keystone species has a much larger effect on its ecosystem than its numbers alone would suggest. Removing it can change the entire community.

Gray wolves are a famous example. Wolves were removed from Yellowstone National Park by the 1920s. Without predators, elk grew numerous and overgrazed young willows and aspens along streams. After wolves were returned in 1995, elk numbers dropped and elk moved around more. Willows and aspens began to recover, giving beavers more food and dam-building material and giving songbirds more nesting sites. A chain of effects like this, passed down through the feeding levels of a food web, is called a trophic cascade.

In Pennsylvania, the beaver is a keystone species of a different kind. By building dams, beavers turn streams into ponds and wetlands that provide habitat for frogs, ducks, fish, and insects.

VOCABULARY
Keystone species — a species that has a much larger effect on its ecosystem than its numbers suggest.
Trophic cascade — a chain of effects that passes through several feeding levels of a food web when one population changes.

LESSON 4: POPULATION GROWTH AND CARRYING CAPACITY

Why don't deer, mice, or dandelions cover the whole Earth? Every population has the potential to grow very fast, but limited resources and other factors keep populations in check.

4.1 Describing Populations

Ecologists describe a population by its size (the number of individuals), its density, and its distribution (how the individuals are spread out). Population density is the number of individuals per unit of area.

Population density = number of individuals ÷ area

Because it is usually impossible to count every individual, ecologists estimate. They may count organisms in a few sample squares called quadrats and multiply, or catch, mark, and release animals and then see how many marked animals are caught again (mark–recapture).

VOCABULARY
Population density — the number of individuals of a species per unit of area.
QUICK CHECK
Wildlife biologists estimate that 240 white-tailed deer live in a 12 km² state game land. What is the population density? Show your work.

4.2 What Changes Population Size

Four processes change the size of a population. Births and immigration (individuals moving in) add individuals. Deaths and emigration (individuals moving out) remove individuals.

Change in population = (births + immigration) − (deaths + emigration)

If more individuals are added than removed, the population grows. If more are removed than added, it shrinks.

VOCABULARY
Birth rate — the number of births in a population over a period of time.
Death rate — the number of deaths in a population over a period of time.
Immigration — the movement of individuals into a population.
Emigration — the movement of individuals out of a population.

4.3 Exponential Growth

When resources are unlimited and nothing limits reproduction, a population shows exponential growth. The population grows by a larger number each generation, because there are more and more individuals reproducing. On a graph, exponential growth forms a J-shaped curve.

Generation0123456
Bacteria (doubling each generation)1248163264

Exponential growth happens in nature only for short periods, such as when a species arrives in a new area with plenty of food and no predators, or when bacteria are placed in fresh nutrient broth.

4.4 Logistic Growth and Carrying Capacity

In most real populations, growth slows down as resources run low. This pattern is logistic growth, which forms an S-shaped curve. Growth starts slowly, speeds up, then slows and levels off. The population levels off at the carrying capacity (K), the largest population an environment can support over a long period of time.

At carrying capacity, births and deaths are roughly balanced. A population may briefly overshoot carrying capacity, but then food runs short or disease spreads, and the population falls back.

VOCABULARY
Exponential growth — population growth that speeds up over time, forming a J-shaped curve, when resources are unlimited.
Logistic growth — population growth that slows and levels off at the carrying capacity, forming an S-shaped curve.
Carrying capacity (K) — the largest population an environment can support over a long period of time.

4.5 Limiting Factors

A limiting factor is anything that controls the growth of a population. Ecologists sort limiting factors into two groups:

Density-dependent factorsDensity-independent factors
Have a stronger effect when a population is crowdedAffect a population the same way no matter how crowded it is
Competition for food, water, spaceFloods, droughts, fires
PredationHurricanes, tornadoes, ice storms
Disease and parasites (spread faster in crowds)Unusually hot or cold weather
VOCABULARY
Limiting factor — anything that controls the growth of a population.
Density-dependent factor — a limiting factor that has a stronger effect when a population is more crowded.
Density-independent factor — a limiting factor that affects a population the same way regardless of its size or density.

4.6 Carrying Capacity at Different Scales

Carrying capacity is not a fixed number. It changes whenever the resources in an environment change, and it can be measured at different scales:

  • A small scale: a single pond may support only a few hundred green frogs, limited by insects to eat and places to lay eggs.
  • A regional scale: Pennsylvania's forests produce huge acorn crops in some years and very few in others. In a big acorn year, the carrying capacity for mice, squirrels, and deer rises, and their populations grow the next year. In a poor year, it falls.
  • A global scale: scientists debate Earth's carrying capacity for humans, which depends on how much food, fresh water, and energy people use.
QUICK CHECK
A population of 200 bluegills in a lake has 50 births, 30 deaths, 5 fish moving in, and 10 fish moving out in one year. What is the population at the end of the year? Show your work.

PART 3

Change and Stability

Succession · Biodiversity · Ecosystem Stability · New Ecosystems

Lesson 5 · Ecological Succession · Lesson 6 · Ecosystem Stability and Change

LESSON 5: ECOLOGICAL SUCCESSION

Ecosystems are always changing. After a volcano, a flood, or a field is abandoned, the community that lives there changes over time in a fairly predictable order.

5.1 What Is Succession?

Ecological succession is the gradual, predictable change in the species that make up a community over time. Succession usually begins after a disturbance, an event such as a fire, flood, storm, or lava flow that removes or damages part of a community.

VOCABULARY
Ecological succession — the gradual, predictable change in the species of a community over time.
Disturbance — an event, such as a fire, flood, or storm, that removes or damages part of a community.

5.2 Primary Succession

Primary succession happens where there is no soil at all, such as on cooled lava, on bare rock left behind by a retreating glacier, or on a newly formed island. The first organisms to arrive are pioneer species, usually lichens and mosses. Lichens release acids that slowly break down rock. When they die, their remains mix with rock particles and begin to form soil.

As soil builds up, small plants can take root. Their roots and dead leaves add more soil, which allows grasses and shrubs to grow, then fast-growing trees, and finally a mature forest. Primary succession can take hundreds to thousands of years.

VOCABULARY
Primary succession — succession that begins in an area with no soil, such as bare rock or cooled lava.
Pioneer species — the first species to live in an area during succession, such as lichens and mosses.

5.3 Secondary Succession

Secondary succession happens where a disturbance has removed the community but left the soil in place, such as after a forest fire, a flood, or when a farm field is abandoned. Because the soil, along with seeds and roots, is already there, secondary succession is much faster than primary succession.

An abandoned farm field in Pennsylvania might change like this:

Years after farming stopsMain plants
1–2Annual weeds such as ragweed and crabgrass
3–10Perennial wildflowers and grasses, such as goldenrod and asters
10–25Shrubs such as sumac and gray dogwood; sun-loving trees begin
25–75Fast-growing trees such as black cherry, red maple, and aspen
75+Shade-tolerant hardwoods such as oaks, sugar maple, and beech

A stable, mature community that changes little over time, as long as conditions stay the same, is sometimes called a climax community. Many ecologists now point out that even mature communities keep changing slowly, especially as disturbances occur.

VOCABULARY
Secondary succession — succession that begins in an area where a disturbance removed the community but left the soil.
Climax community — a stable, mature community that changes little as long as conditions stay the same.
QUICK CHECK
Which happens faster after a disturbance, primary succession or secondary succession? Explain why.

5.4 Each Community Prepares the Way

At each stage of succession, the organisms change the abiotic conditions. They add soil, hold moisture, and create shade. These changes make the area better for the next group of species and worse for the species already there. Sun-loving trees, for example, cannot sprout in the deep shade they themselves create, so shade-tolerant trees slowly replace them.

LESSON 6: ECOSYSTEM STABILITY AND CHANGE

Some ecosystems stay much the same for hundreds of years, while others change quickly. Ecologists use numbers and evidence to measure biodiversity and to explain why ecosystems stay stable, recover, or change into something new.

6.1 Measuring Biodiversity

Biodiversity is the variety of life in an area. One way to measure it is species richness, the number of different species. But richness does not tell the whole story. Species evenness describes how equally the individuals are divided among those species.

Both meadows have a species richness of 4. In Meadow 2, however, almost every plant is goldenrod, so a walk through it would feel like a goldenrod field. Meadow 1 is more diverse.

Ecologists combine richness and evenness in a diversity index. A common one is Simpson's diversity index:

D = 1 − Σ (n ÷ N)²

Here n is the number of individuals of one species and N is the total number of individuals. Square each species' fraction, add the squares, and subtract from 1. D ranges from 0 (no diversity) to almost 1 (very high diversity).

Meadow 1Meadow 2
Fractions (n ÷ N)0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.250.85, 0.05, 0.05, 0.05
Sum of squares0.0625 × 4 = 0.250.7225 + 0.0025 × 3 = 0.73
D = 1 − sum0.750.27
VOCABULARY
Biodiversity — the variety of life in an area.
Species richness — the number of different species in an area.
Species evenness — how equally individuals are divided among the species in an area.
Diversity index — a number that combines species richness and evenness to measure biodiversity.
QUICK CHECK
A small stream sample contains 50 mayfly nymphs and 50 caddisfly larvae. Calculate Simpson's diversity index. Show your work.

6.2 Stability Under Stable Conditions

When conditions stay fairly steady, an ecosystem tends to keep relatively consistent numbers and types of organisms. Populations still rise and fall, but they move up and down around an average. Complex interactions hold them in check: if a prey population grows, predators have more food and eat more prey; if a plant is overgrazed, the herbivores that eat it go hungry and decline.

Ecosystems with more biodiversity and more complex food webs are usually more stable. If one food source disappears, consumers can switch to another, and if one species declines, others can fill its role.

VOCABULARY
Ecosystem stability — the ability of an ecosystem to keep relatively consistent numbers and types of organisms over time.
Resilience — the ability of an ecosystem to recover after a disturbance.

6.3 Disturbance and Recovery

Natural disturbances such as fires, floods, storms, and droughts are a normal part of many ecosystems. After a moderate disturbance, a resilient ecosystem recovers through secondary succession and returns to a community much like the one before.

6.4 When Conditions Change: A New Ecosystem

If conditions change too much, or change permanently, the old community may not come back. Instead, a new ecosystem forms with different species. The point at which an ecosystem shifts to a new state is sometimes called a tipping point.

  • When beavers dam a stream, the flooded forest dies, and the area becomes a pond and then a wetland meadow, with frogs, ducks, and cattails in place of trees.
  • If a region's climate becomes much drier for many decades, a forest can gradually give way to grassland.
  • If an introduced pest kills nearly all of one dominant tree, as the chestnut blight did to American chestnut trees in Pennsylvania's forests in the early 1900s, the forest community reorganizes around other species, such as oaks.
VOCABULARY
Tipping point — the point at which a change in conditions causes an ecosystem to shift into a new, different state.
Evaluating a Claim
Scientists judge claims using claim, evidence, and reasoning. Claim: "The forest at Site A is stable." Evidence: Tree surveys every 10 years for 60 years show the same five dominant species, and the number of trees stayed between 410 and 450 per hectare. Reasoning: Numbers and types of organisms that stay relatively consistent over many years are the sign of a stable ecosystem. A strong evaluation asks whether the evidence covers enough time, whether the data were collected the same way each time, and whether conditions really stayed the same.
QUICK CHECK
A beaver builds a dam, and over 20 years a stretch of forest becomes a wetland. Is this ecosystem resilient, or has it shifted to a new ecosystem? Use evidence from the example.

VOCABULARY GLOSSARY

Every key term from Parts 1–3, in alphabetical order, for quick reference while studying.

Abiotic factora nonliving physical or chemical part of an ecosystem.
Biodiversitythe variety of life in an area.
Biomea large region with a similar climate and similar kinds of communities.
Biosphereall the parts of Earth where life exists.
Biotic factora living or once-living part of an ecosystem.
Birth ratethe number of births in a population over a period of time.
Carrying capacity (K)the largest population an environment can support over a long period of time.
Climatethe average temperature and precipitation of an area over many years.
Climax communitya stable, mature community that changes little as long as conditions stay the same.
Commensalisma relationship in which one species benefits and the other is not affected.
Communityall the populations of different species that live and interact in an area.
Competitionan interaction in which organisms need the same limited resource.
Competitive exclusion principlethe idea that two species cannot occupy exactly the same niche in the same place for long.
Death ratethe number of deaths in a population over a period of time.
Density-dependent factora limiting factor that has a stronger effect when a population is more crowded.
Density-independent factora limiting factor that affects a population the same way regardless of its size or density.
Disturbancean event, such as a fire, flood, or storm, that removes or damages part of a community.
Diversity indexa number that combines species richness and evenness to measure biodiversity.
Ecological successionthe gradual, predictable change in the species of a community over time.
Ecologythe study of interactions among organisms and between organisms and their environment.
Ecosystema community plus the nonliving parts of its environment.
Ecosystem stabilitythe ability of an ecosystem to keep relatively consistent numbers and types of organisms over time.
Emigrationthe movement of individuals out of a population.
Exponential growthpopulation growth that speeds up over time, forming a J-shaped curve, when resources are unlimited.
Fundamental nichethe full range of conditions and resources a species could use.
Habitatthe place where an organism lives and gets what it needs to survive.
Herbivoryan interaction in which an animal eats plants or parts of plants.
Immigrationthe movement of individuals into a population.
Interspecific competitioncompetition between members of different species.
Intraspecific competitioncompetition between members of the same species.
Keystone speciesa species that has a much larger effect on its ecosystem than its numbers suggest.
Limiting factoranything that controls the growth of a population.
Logistic growthpopulation growth that slows and levels off at the carrying capacity, forming an S-shaped curve.
Mutualisma relationship in which both species benefit.
Nichean organism's role in its ecosystem, including what it eats, where and when it feeds, and the conditions it can tolerate.
Organismone individual living thing.
Parasitisma relationship in which one species (the parasite) benefits and the other (the host) is harmed.
Pioneer speciesthe first species to live in an area during succession, such as lichens and mosses.
Populationall the members of one species living in the same area at the same time.
Population densitythe number of individuals of a species per unit of area.
Predationan interaction in which one organism kills and eats another.
Primary successionsuccession that begins in an area with no soil, such as bare rock or cooled lava.
Range of tolerancethe range of an abiotic factor, such as temperature, within which an organism can survive.
Realized nichethe part of the fundamental niche a species actually uses because of competition and other interactions.
Resiliencethe ability of an ecosystem to recover after a disturbance.
Resource partitioningthe division of resources among similar species so that each uses them in a different way, place, or time.
Secondary successionsuccession that begins in an area where a disturbance removed the community but left the soil.
Species evennesshow equally individuals are divided among the species in an area.
Species richnessthe number of different species in an area.
Symbiosisa close, long-term relationship between two different species.
Tipping pointthe point at which a change in conditions causes an ecosystem to shift into a new, different state.
Trophic cascadea chain of effects that passes through several feeding levels of a food web when one population changes.

11. (A) Secondary succession, because the soil is still present from farming. (B) Annual weeds → perennial wildflowers and grasses such as goldenrod → shrubs such as sumac → fast-growing trees such as black cherry and aspen → shade-tolerant hardwoods such as oak, maple, and beech. 12. (A) Examples: surveys over many years show the same dominant tree species; population counts of trees, deer, or birds rise and fall around a steady average; species richness and diversity index stay about the same over decades. (B) Example: a permanent change such as decades of much drier climate, a beaver dam flooding the forest, or a pest killing a dominant tree. Because the abiotic conditions (or a key species) are permanently changed, the original community can no longer survive there, so the ecosystem passes a tipping point and reorganizes into a new one, such as a grassland or wetland.

Quick Checks (sample answers)

Lesson 1: Population. She is counting only one species (eastern hemlock) in one area at one time.

Lesson 1: The place with 25 cm of rain is likely a desert or dry grassland, because few plants can grow with so little water. The place with 150 cm is likely a forest (such as a temperate deciduous forest), because plentiful rain supports trees.

Lesson 2: Brown trout. As the water warms, it moves outside the brook trout's range of tolerance but stays within the brown trout's, so brown trout can keep feeding and reproducing while brook trout decline.

Lesson 3: Lynx depend on hares for food. When hares become plentiful, lynx survive and reproduce better, but it takes time for their population to grow, so the lynx peak lags behind the hare peak.

Lesson 4: 240 deer ÷ 12 km² = 20 deer per km².

Lesson 4: Change = (50 + 5) − (30 + 10) = 55 − 40 = +15. New population = 200 + 15 = 215 bluegills.

Lesson 5: Secondary succession is faster, because soil (and often seeds and roots) is already present. Primary succession must first build soil from bare rock, which takes hundreds of years.

Lesson 6: Each fraction is 50 ÷ 100 = 0.5. Sum of squares = 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5. D = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5.

Lesson 6: It has shifted to a new ecosystem. The flooding permanently changed the abiotic conditions (standing water), so the original forest community did not return; instead wetland species such as cattails, frogs, and ducks replaced the trees.

PART 1

Organization of Ecosystems

Levels of Organization · Biotic and Abiotic Factors · Biomes · Habitats · Niches

Lesson 1 · Levels of Ecological Organization · Lesson 2 · Habitats and Niches

LESSON 1: LEVELS OF ECOLOGICAL ORGANIZATION

Ecology is the study of how living things interact with each other and with their surroundings. Ecologists study life at many sizes. They can study one fish or the whole planet.

1.1 From Organism to Biosphere

Ecologists sort the living world into levels. Each level includes the level before it, plus more.

  • Organism — one living thing. Example: one brook trout.
  • Population — all the members of one species in one area. Example: all the brook trout in one stream.
  • Community — all the different species living together in one area. Example: the trout, crayfish, insects, algae, and plants in the stream.
  • Ecosystem — the community plus the nonliving things around it, like water, rocks, and sunlight.
  • Biome — a large region with the same climate and similar living things. Most of Pennsylvania is a temperate deciduous forest biome.
  • Biosphere — every place on Earth where life is found.
VOCABULARY
Ecology — the study of how living things interact with each other and their surroundings.
Organism — one living thing.
Population — all the members of one species in one area.
Community — all the different species living in one area.
VOCABULARY
Ecosystem — a community plus the nonliving things around it.
Biome — a large region with the same climate and similar living things.
Biosphere — all the places on Earth where life is found.
QUICK CHECK
A scientist counts every hemlock tree in one part of a forest. Which level is she studying? How do you know? (Hint: She is counting only one kind of tree.)

1.2 Biotic and Abiotic Factors

Every ecosystem has living parts and nonliving parts.

  • Biotic factors are living things, or things that were once alive. Examples: plants, animals, fungi, bacteria, dead leaves.
  • Abiotic factors are nonliving things. Examples: sunlight, temperature, water, soil, oxygen.
EcosystemBiotic factors (living)Abiotic factors (nonliving)
Pennsylvania mountain streamBrook trout, insects, crayfish, algae, trees on the bankCold water, oxygen in the water, rocks, shade
Farm fieldCorn, earthworms, deer, weedsSunlight, rain, soil, temperature
Forest floorFungi, salamanders, ferns, fallen leavesMoisture, soil, shade

Biotic and abiotic factors affect each other. Brook trout need cold water. Trees on the bank shade the stream and keep the water cold. If the trees are cut down, the water gets warmer. Warm water holds less oxygen, so the trout may die.

VOCABULARY
Biotic factor — a living or once-living part of an ecosystem.
Abiotic factor — a nonliving part of an ecosystem.

1.3 Biomes

The biome in a place depends mostly on its climate. Climate is the usual temperature and rainfall in a place over many years. Climate decides which plants can grow. The plants decide which animals can live there.

BiomeClimateLiving things
TundraVery cold; little rain or snowMosses, lichens, caribou
TaigaLong, cold wintersSpruce trees, moose, lynx
Temperate deciduous forestFour seasons; lots of rainOak, maple, deer, black bear
GrasslandHot summers, cold winters; some rainGrasses, bison
DesertVery dryCacti, lizards
Tropical rain forestWarm all year; lots of rainVines, monkeys, the most species
VOCABULARY
Climate — the usual temperature and rainfall in a place over many years.
QUICK CHECK
Two places have the same temperature. One gets very little rain. The other gets a lot of rain. Which place could be a desert? Which could be a forest? Why?

LESSON 2: HABITATS AND NICHES

A deer and a woodpecker can live in the same forest. But they live very different lives. Ecologists use two words to describe this: habitat and niche.

2.1 Habitat

A habitat is the place where an organism lives. It gives the organism food, water, and shelter. A habitat is like an organism's address. The habitat of a brook trout is a cold, clean stream.

2.2 Niche

A niche is an organism's role, or job, in its ecosystem. A niche includes:

  • what the organism eats, and what eats it
  • where and when it looks for food
  • how it has young
  • the conditions it can live in, like how hot or cold

Each species can live only in a certain range of tolerance. For example, brook trout need water colder than about 20 °C. If the water gets too warm, the trout get stressed and may die.

VOCABULARY
Habitat — the place where an organism lives (its address).
Niche — an organism's role in its ecosystem (its job).
Range of tolerance — the conditions, like temperature, that an organism can live in.

2.3 Competitive Exclusion

What if two species have the same niche? A scientist named G. F. Gause tested this. He put two kinds of tiny Paramecium in one container with the same food. Alone, each kind grew well. Together, one kind always won. The other kind died out.

This is the competitive exclusion principle: two species cannot have exactly the same niche in the same place for long. One species will win.

2.4 Resource Partitioning

Similar species often share by dividing up resources. A scientist studied small birds called warblers. Several kinds ate insects in the same spruce trees. But each kind fed in a different part of the tree. This is called resource partitioning. Because their niches are a little different, all the warblers can live in the same tree.

VOCABULARY
Competitive exclusion principle — two species cannot have exactly the same niche in the same place for long.
Resource partitioning — similar species share resources by using them in different ways, places, or times.

2.5 Fundamental and Realized Niches

The fundamental niche is everything a species could use. But competition often stops a species from using all of it. The realized niche is the part it actually uses. For example, one kind of barnacle could live on all the rocks of a shore. A stronger barnacle pushes it off the lower rocks. So it lives only on the upper rocks.

VOCABULARY
Fundamental niche — everything a species could use.
Realized niche — the part of its niche a species actually uses.
QUICK CHECK
Brook trout and brown trout eat the same insects. Brown trout can live in warmer water than brook trout. If the stream gets warmer, which trout will stay? Use the words range of tolerance.

PART 2

Interactions and Populations

Competition · Predation · Symbiosis · Population Growth · Carrying Capacity

Lesson 3 · Ecological Interactions · Lesson 4 · Population Growth and Carrying Capacity

LESSON 3: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS

No organism lives alone. Organisms compete, eat each other, or live together as partners. These interactions change the size of every population.

3.1 Competition

Competition happens when organisms need the same thing and there is not enough of it. They may need food, water, light, space, or mates. Competition hurts both sides, because each one gets less.

  • Intraspecific competition is between members of the same species. Example: two male deer fighting over a mate.
  • Interspecific competition is between different species. Example: maple and oak seedlings both need sunlight.
VOCABULARY
Competition — when organisms need the same thing and there is not enough.
Intraspecific competition — competition within the same species.
Interspecific competition — competition between different species.

3.2 Predation and Herbivory

In predation, one animal (the predator) kills and eats another animal (the prey). Example: a hawk catches a mouse. In herbivory, an animal eats plants. Example: deer eat young trees.

Prey have ways to stay safe, like hiding colors (camouflage), speed, spines, or poison. Predators have ways to catch prey, like sharp eyes, speed, and claws.

Predator and prey numbers often go up and down together. When there are many snowshoe hares, lynx have lots of food, so more lynx survive. Then the many lynx eat many hares, so hares go down. With less food, lynx go down too. Then the cycle starts again.

VOCABULARY
Predation — when one animal kills and eats another.
Herbivory — when an animal eats plants.
QUICK CHECK
Look at the graph. Why does the lynx line go up a little after the hare line goes up? (Hint: Lynx eat hares.)

3.3 Symbiosis

Symbiosis is when two different species live closely together for a long time. There are three types:

TypeSpecies 1Species 2Example
Mutualism+ helped+ helpedBees get nectar. Flowers get pollinated.
Commensalism+ helped0 not affectedBarnacles ride on a whale. The whale is not affected.
Parasitism+ helped (parasite)− harmed (host)A tick drinks a deer's blood.
VOCABULARY
Symbiosis — two different species living closely together.
Mutualism — both species are helped.
Commensalism — one species is helped and the other is not affected.
Parasitism — one species (the parasite) is helped and the other (the host) is harmed.

3.4 Keystone Species and Trophic Cascades

A keystone species has a very big effect on its ecosystem. If it is removed, the whole community can change.

Gray wolves are an example. Wolves were removed from Yellowstone Park long ago. Without wolves, elk ate too many young trees by the streams. In 1995, wolves were brought back. Elk numbers went down, and the elk moved around more. The trees grew back. Then beavers and songbirds had more food and homes. This chain of changes through a food web is called a trophic cascade.

In Pennsylvania, the beaver is a keystone species too. Beaver dams turn streams into ponds and wetlands. These make homes for frogs, ducks, fish, and insects.

VOCABULARY
Keystone species — a species with a very big effect on its ecosystem.
Trophic cascade — a chain of changes through a food web when one population changes.

LESSON 4: POPULATION GROWTH AND CARRYING CAPACITY

Why don't deer or mice cover the whole Earth? Every population can grow fast. But limited food, space, and other things keep populations in check.

4.1 Describing Populations

Ecologists describe a population by its size (how many) and its density (how crowded). Population density is the number of individuals in a certain area.

Population density = number of individuals ÷ area

Scientists usually cannot count every organism. So they count a few small squares and multiply. Or they catch, mark, and release animals, then see how many marked animals they catch again.

VOCABULARY
Population density — the number of individuals in a certain area.
QUICK CHECK
240 deer live in an area of 12 km². What is the population density? Show your work.

Density = ______ deer ÷ ______ km² = ______ deer per km².

4.2 What Changes Population Size

Four things change a population's size:

  • Births and immigration (moving in) add individuals.
  • Deaths and emigration (moving out) remove individuals.

Change in population = (births + immigration) − (deaths + emigration)

VOCABULARY
Birth rate — how many are born in a population over a period of time.
Death rate — how many die in a population over a period of time.
Immigration — moving into a population.
Emigration — moving out of a population.

4.3 Exponential Growth

If there is unlimited food and space, a population grows faster and faster. This is exponential growth. On a graph, it makes a J-shaped curve.

Generation0123456
Bacteria (doubling)1248163264

In nature, exponential growth lasts only a short time. It can happen when a species moves to a new place with lots of food and no predators.

4.4 Logistic Growth and Carrying Capacity

In most populations, growth slows down when food and space start to run out. This is logistic growth. It makes an S-shaped curve. Growth starts slow, speeds up, then slows and levels off.

The population levels off at the carrying capacity (K). That is the largest population an area can support for a long time.

VOCABULARY
Exponential growth — growth that gets faster and faster; makes a J-curve.
Logistic growth — growth that slows and levels off; makes an S-curve.
Carrying capacity (K) — the largest population an area can support for a long time.

4.5 Limiting Factors

A limiting factor is anything that keeps a population from growing. There are two kinds:

Density-dependent factorsDensity-independent factors
Stronger when a population is crowdedSame effect no matter how crowded
Competition for food, water, spaceFloods, droughts, fires
PredatorsStorms and hurricanes
Disease (spreads fast in crowds)Very hot or very cold weather
VOCABULARY
Limiting factor — anything that keeps a population from growing.
Density-dependent factor — a limiting factor that is stronger when a population is crowded.
Density-independent factor — a limiting factor that has the same effect no matter how crowded.

4.6 Carrying Capacity at Different Scales

Carrying capacity can change. When there is more food, the carrying capacity goes up. When there is less food, it goes down.

  • Small scale: one pond can support only so many frogs.
  • Regional scale: some years, Pennsylvania oak trees make lots of acorns. Then more mice, squirrels, and deer can live there the next year.
  • Global scale: scientists ask how many people Earth can support. It depends on how much food, water, and energy people use.

PART 3

Change and Stability

Succession · Biodiversity · Ecosystem Stability · New Ecosystems

Lesson 5 · Ecological Succession · Lesson 6 · Ecosystem Stability and Change

LESSON 5: ECOLOGICAL SUCCESSION

Ecosystems are always changing. After a fire, a flood, or a volcano, the living things in a place change over time. They change in an order we can predict.

5.1 What Is Succession?

Ecological succession is the slow change in which species live in a place over time. Succession usually starts after a disturbance. A disturbance is an event, like a fire, flood, or storm, that destroys part of a community.

VOCABULARY
Ecological succession — the slow, predictable change in which species live in a place over time.
Disturbance — an event, like a fire or flood, that destroys part of a community.

5.2 Primary Succession

Primary succession happens where there is no soil. Examples: cooled lava, or bare rock left by a melting glacier.

  1. Pioneer species come first. These are usually lichens and mosses.
  2. Lichens make acids that slowly break rock into tiny pieces. When lichens die, they mix with the rock pieces. This starts to make soil.
  3. Small plants grow in the thin soil. They add more soil when they die.
  4. Grasses and shrubs grow. Then fast-growing trees. Finally, a mature forest.

Primary succession can take hundreds or thousands of years.

VOCABULARY
Primary succession — succession that starts where there is no soil, like bare rock.
Pioneer species — the first species to live in a new area, like lichens and mosses.

5.3 Secondary Succession

Secondary succession happens where the soil is still there. Examples: after a forest fire, a flood, or when a farmer stops using a field. Soil, seeds, and roots are already there. So secondary succession is much faster than primary succession.

An old farm field in Pennsylvania might change like this:

Years after farming stopsMain plants
1–2Weeds like ragweed and crabgrass
3–10Wildflowers and grasses, like goldenrod
10–25Shrubs like sumac; small sun-loving trees
25–75Fast-growing trees like black cherry and aspen
75+Oaks, maples, and beech trees

A mature community that stays about the same is called a climax community.

VOCABULARY
Secondary succession — succession that starts where the soil is still there.
Climax community — a mature community that stays about the same over time.
QUICK CHECK
Which is faster: primary succession or secondary succession? Why?

______ succession is faster because ______ .

5.4 Each Community Prepares the Way

Each group of living things changes the place. They add soil, hold water, and make shade. These changes help the next group of species grow. For example, sun-loving trees make shade. Their own seedlings cannot grow in the shade, but oak and maple seedlings can. So oaks and maples slowly take over.

LESSON 6: ECOSYSTEM STABILITY AND CHANGE

Some ecosystems stay the same for hundreds of years. Others change fast. Ecologists use numbers and evidence to tell which is which.

6.1 Measuring Biodiversity

Biodiversity means the variety of life in an area. Ecologists measure it in two ways:

  • Species richness — how many different species there are.
  • Species evenness — how equal the numbers of each species are.

Both meadows have 4 species, so their richness is the same. But Meadow 2 is almost all goldenrod. Meadow 1 is more even, so it is more diverse.

A diversity index is one number that measures diversity. Simpson's diversity index uses this formula:

D = 1 − Σ (n ÷ N)²

  • n = number of one species. N = total number of all organisms.
  • Step 1: Find n ÷ N for each species.
  • Step 2: Square each answer (multiply it by itself).
  • Step 3: Add the squares.
  • Step 4: Subtract the total from 1.
  • D close to 0 = low diversity. D close to 1 = high diversity.
Meadow 1Meadow 2
Step 1: n ÷ N0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.250.85, 0.05, 0.05, 0.05
Steps 2–3: add the squares0.0625 × 4 = 0.250.7225 + 0.0025 × 3 = 0.73
Step 4: D = 1 − total0.750.27
VOCABULARY
Biodiversity — the variety of life in an area.
Species richness — how many different species are in an area.
Species evenness — how equal the numbers of each species are.
Diversity index — one number that measures richness and evenness together.
QUICK CHECK
A stream sample has 50 mayflies and 50 caddisflies. Find Simpson's diversity index. Show your work.

n ÷ N = 50 ÷ 100 = ______ . Squares: ______ + ______ = ______ . D = 1 − ______ = ______ .

6.2 Stability Under Stable Conditions

When conditions stay steady, an ecosystem keeps about the same numbers and kinds of living things. Populations still go up and down, but they stay near an average. For example, if prey increase, predators have more food and eat more prey. Then the prey go back down.

Ecosystems with more biodiversity are usually more stable. If one food runs out, animals can eat something else.

VOCABULARY
Ecosystem stability — when an ecosystem keeps about the same numbers and kinds of living things over time.
Resilience — an ecosystem's ability to recover after a disturbance.

6.3 Disturbance and Recovery

Fires, floods, storms, and droughts happen naturally. After a medium-sized disturbance, a resilient ecosystem recovers. It goes through secondary succession and becomes much like it was before.

6.4 When Conditions Change: A New Ecosystem

If conditions change too much, or change forever, the old community may not come back. A new ecosystem forms instead. The point where this happens is called a tipping point.

  • Beavers build a dam. The water floods the forest, and the trees die. The area becomes a pond and then a wetland with frogs, ducks, and cattails.
  • A place becomes much drier for many years. A forest slowly turns into a grassland.
  • A disease kills almost all of one important tree. In the early 1900s, chestnut blight killed most American chestnut trees in Pennsylvania. The forest changed, and oaks took their place.
VOCABULARY
Tipping point — the point where an ecosystem changes into a new, different ecosystem.
Evaluating a Claim
Scientists check claims using claim, evidence, and reasoning.
Claim: "The forest at Site A is stable."
Evidence: Every 10 years for 60 years, the same five kinds of trees were most common. The number of trees stayed between 410 and 450 per hectare.
Reasoning: When the numbers and kinds of living things stay about the same for many years, the ecosystem is stable.
QUICK CHECK
Beavers build a dam. After 20 years, part of a forest is now a wetland. Did the forest recover, or is it a new ecosystem? Give evidence.

It is ______ because ______ .

VOCABULARY GLOSSARY

Every key term from Parts 1–3, in alphabetical order, for quick reference while studying.

Abiotic factora nonliving part of an ecosystem.
Biodiversitythe variety of life in an area.
Biomea large region with the same climate and similar living things.
Biosphereall the places on Earth where life is found.
Biotic factora living or once-living part of an ecosystem.
Birth ratehow many are born in a population over a period of time.
Carrying capacity (K)the largest population an area can support for a long time.
Climatethe usual temperature and rainfall in a place over many years.
Climax communitya mature community that stays about the same over time.
Commensalismone species is helped and the other is not affected.
Communityall the different species living in one area.
Competitionwhen organisms need the same thing and there is not enough.
Competitive exclusion principletwo species cannot have exactly the same niche in the same place for long.
Death ratehow many die in a population over a period of time.
Density-dependent factora limiting factor that is stronger when a population is crowded.
Density-independent factora limiting factor that has the same effect no matter how crowded.
Disturbancean event, like a fire or flood, that destroys part of a community.
Diversity indexone number that measures richness and evenness together.
Ecological successionthe slow, predictable change in which species live in a place over time.
Ecologythe study of how living things interact with each other and their surroundings.
Ecosystema community plus the nonliving things around it.
Ecosystem stabilitywhen an ecosystem keeps about the same numbers and kinds of living things over time.
Emigrationmoving out of a population.
Exponential growthgrowth that gets faster and faster; makes a J-curve.
Fundamental nicheeverything a species could use.
Habitatthe place where an organism lives (its address).
Herbivorywhen an animal eats plants.
Immigrationmoving into a population.
Interspecific competitioncompetition between different species.
Intraspecific competitioncompetition within the same species.
Keystone speciesa species with a very big effect on its ecosystem.
Limiting factoranything that keeps a population from growing.
Logistic growthgrowth that slows and levels off; makes an S-curve.
Mutualismboth species are helped.
Nichean organism's role in its ecosystem (its job).
Organismone living thing.
Parasitismone species (the parasite) is helped and the other (the host) is harmed.
Pioneer speciesthe first species to live in a new area, like lichens and mosses.
Populationall the members of one species in one area.
Population densitythe number of individuals in a certain area.
Predationwhen one animal kills and eats another.
Primary successionsuccession that starts where there is no soil, like bare rock.
Range of tolerancethe conditions, like temperature, that an organism can live in.
Realized nichethe part of its niche a species actually uses.
Resiliencean ecosystem's ability to recover after a disturbance.
Resource partitioningsimilar species share resources by using them in different ways, places, or times.
Secondary successionsuccession that starts where the soil is still there.
Species evennesshow equal the numbers of each species are.
Species richnesshow many different species are in an area.
Symbiosistwo different species living closely together.
Tipping pointthe point where an ecosystem changes into a new, different ecosystem.
Trophic cascadea chain of changes through a food web when one population changes.

Quick Checks (sample answers)

Lesson 1: Population. She is counting only one species (hemlock) in one area.

Lesson 1: The place with very little rain could be a desert, because few plants can grow without water. The place with a lot of rain could be a forest, because trees need a lot of water.

Lesson 2: Brown trout. The warmer water is outside the brook trout's range of tolerance but still inside the brown trout's range of tolerance.

Lesson 3: Lynx eat hares. When there are more hares, more lynx survive and have young. That takes time, so the lynx go up after the hares.

Lesson 4: 240 ÷ 12 = 20 deer per km².

Lesson 4: Change = (50 + 5) − (30 + 10) = 55 − 40 = +15. New population = 200 + 15 = 215 bluegills.

Lesson 5: Secondary succession is faster, because the soil is already there. Primary succession must make soil from bare rock first, which takes a very long time.

Lesson 6: Each fraction is 50 ÷ 100 = 0.5. Squares: 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5. D = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5.

Lesson 6: It is a new ecosystem. The flooding changed the conditions for good (standing water), so the forest did not come back. Wetland species like cattails, frogs, and ducks replaced the trees.

PARTE 1

La organización de los ecosistemas

Niveles de organización · Factores bióticos y abióticos · Biomas · Hábitats · Nichos

Lección 1 · Niveles de organización ecológica · Lección 2 · Hábitats y nichos

LECCIÓN 1: NIVELES DE ORGANIZACIÓN ECOLÓGICA

La ecología es el estudio de cómo los organismos interactúan entre sí y con su medio ambiente. Los ecólogos estudian la vida a muchas escalas distintas, desde una sola trucha de arroyo en un río de Pensilvania hasta el planeta entero.

1.1 Del organismo a la biosfera

Los ecólogos organizan el mundo vivo en niveles. Cada nivel incluye todo lo del nivel anterior, más algo adicional.

  • Organismo — un solo ser vivo individual, como una trucha de arroyo.
  • Población — todos los miembros de una misma especie que viven en la misma área al mismo tiempo, como todas las truchas de un arroyo.
  • Comunidad — todas las poblaciones de distintas especies que viven e interactúan en un área: las truchas, los cangrejos de río, las efímeras, las algas y las plantas de la orilla.
  • Ecosistema — la comunidad más las partes sin vida de su medio ambiente, como el agua, las rocas, la luz solar y la temperatura.
  • Bioma — una gran región de la Tierra con un clima parecido y tipos de comunidades parecidas, como el bosque templado caducifolio que cubre la mayor parte de Pensilvania.
  • Biosfera — todas las partes de la Tierra donde existe vida, desde el fondo del océano hasta la parte alta de la atmósfera.
VOCABULARIO
Ecología — el estudio de las interacciones entre los organismos y entre los organismos y su medio ambiente.
Organismo — un solo ser vivo individual.
Población — todos los miembros de una misma especie que viven en la misma área al mismo tiempo.
Comunidad — todas las poblaciones de distintas especies que viven e interactúan en un área.
VOCABULARIO
Ecosistema — una comunidad más las partes sin vida de su medio ambiente.
Bioma — una gran región con un clima parecido y tipos de comunidades parecidas.
Biosfera — todas las partes de la Tierra donde existe vida.
COMPRUEBA LO APRENDIDO
Una bióloga cuenta todos los árboles de tsuga del este en una parcela de bosque de una hectárea. ¿Qué nivel de organización está estudiando? Explica cómo lo sabes.

1.2 Factores bióticos y abióticos

Todo ecosistema tiene partes vivas y partes sin vida. Los factores bióticos son las partes vivas (o que estuvieron vivas) de un ecosistema, como las plantas, los animales, los hongos, las bacterias y las hojas muertas. Los factores abióticos son las partes físicas y químicas sin vida, como la luz solar, la temperatura, el agua, el suelo, el oxígeno y el pH.

EcosistemaFactores bióticosFactores abióticos
Arroyo de montaña de PensilvaniaTruchas de arroyo, ninfas de efímera, cangrejos de río, algas, tsugas en la orillaAgua fría, oxígeno disuelto, velocidad de la corriente, rocas, sombra
Campo de cultivoMaíz, lombrices, venados, bacterias del suelo, malezasLuz solar, lluvia, nutrientes del suelo, temperatura
Suelo del bosqueHongos, salamandras, helechos, hojas caídasHumedad, pH del suelo, sombra

Los factores bióticos y abióticos se afectan entre sí constantemente. El agua fría y rica en oxígeno permite que vivan las truchas de arroyo. A su vez, las tsugas de la orilla dan sombra al arroyo y mantienen el agua fría. Si se talan los árboles, el agua se calienta, contiene menos oxígeno y las truchas pueden desaparecer.

VOCABULARIO
Factor biótico — una parte viva, o que estuvo viva, de un ecosistema.
Factor abiótico — una parte física o química sin vida de un ecosistema.

1.3 Los biomas

El tipo de bioma de un lugar depende sobre todo de su clima, es decir, la temperatura y la precipitación promedio durante muchos años. El clima determina qué plantas pueden crecer, y las plantas determinan qué animales pueden vivir allí.

BiomaClimaOrganismos típicos
TundraMuy frío; poca precipitación; suelo congelado (permafrost)Musgos, líquenes, caribúes, zorro ártico
Taiga (bosque boreal)Inviernos largos y fríos; precipitación moderadaAbetos, píceas, alces, linces
Bosque templado caducifolioCuatro estaciones; mucha lluviaRobles, arces, venado cola blanca, oso negro
PraderaVeranos calurosos, inviernos fríos; lluvia moderadaPastos, bisontes, perritos de la pradera
DesiertoMuy seco; días calurosos, noches frescasCactus, lagartijas, ratas canguro
Bosque tropical lluviosoCálido todo el año; lluvias muy abundantesLianas, orquídeas, monos; la mayor cantidad de especies de todos los biomas
VOCABULARIO
Clima — la temperatura y la precipitación promedio de un área durante muchos años.
COMPRUEBA LO APRENDIDO
Dos lugares tienen la misma temperatura promedio. Uno recibe 25 cm de lluvia al año y el otro recibe 150 cm. Predice qué bioma podría ser cada lugar y explica tu razonamiento.

LECCIÓN 2: HÁBITATS Y NICHOS

Un venado cola blanca y un pájaro carpintero picamaderos pueden vivir en el mismo bosque de Pensilvania y aun así llevar vidas muy distintas. Los ecólogos describen estas diferencias con dos ideas: hábitat y nicho.

2.1 El hábitat

El hábitat de un organismo es el lugar donde vive: el área que le da el alimento, el agua, el refugio y las demás condiciones que necesita. El hábitat es como la dirección del organismo. El hábitat de la trucha de arroyo es un arroyo frío, limpio y con mucho oxígeno.

2.2 El nicho

El nicho de un organismo es su papel en el ecosistema: todo lo relacionado con cómo vive y cómo usa su hábitat. Si el hábitat es la dirección, el nicho es el oficio. Un nicho incluye:

  • qué come el organismo y qué lo come a él
  • dónde y cuándo se alimenta (en la copa de los árboles o en el suelo, de día o de noche)
  • cómo y cuándo se reproduce
  • el rango de condiciones abióticas, como la temperatura y el pH, en las que puede sobrevivir

Cada especie solo puede sobrevivir dentro de cierto rango de tolerancia para cada factor abiótico. Por ejemplo, a la trucha de arroyo le va mejor en agua a menos de unos 20 °C. Fuera de su rango de tolerancia, un organismo se estresa, deja de reproducirse o muere.

VOCABULARIO
Hábitat — el lugar donde vive un organismo y obtiene lo que necesita para sobrevivir.
Nicho — el papel de un organismo en su ecosistema, que incluye qué come, dónde y cuándo se alimenta y qué condiciones tolera.
Rango de tolerancia — el rango de un factor abiótico, como la temperatura, dentro del cual un organismo puede sobrevivir.

2.3 La exclusión competitiva

¿Qué pasa cuando dos especies intentan ocupar el mismo nicho? En la década de 1930, el científico G. F. Gause cultivó dos especies de Paramecium en el mismo recipiente con el mismo alimento. Por separado, a cada especie le iba bien. Juntas, una especie siempre superaba a la otra y la eliminaba por completo.

Esto dio origen al principio de exclusión competitiva: dos especies no pueden ocupar exactamente el mismo nicho en el mismo lugar por mucho tiempo. Una aprovechará mejor los recursos compartidos y acabará excluyendo a la otra.

2.4 La repartición de recursos

Las especies parecidas suelen evitar la exclusión competitiva repartiéndose los recursos. En la década de 1950, el ecólogo Robert MacArthur estudió varias especies de reinitas que comían insectos en los mismos abetos. Descubrió que cada especie se alimentaba en una parte distinta del árbol. Esto se llama repartición de recursos. Como cada especie tiene un nicho un poco distinto, todas pueden vivir en el mismo hábitat.

VOCABULARIO
Principio de exclusión competitiva — la idea de que dos especies no pueden ocupar exactamente el mismo nicho en el mismo lugar por mucho tiempo.
Repartición de recursos — la división de los recursos entre especies parecidas para que cada una los use de distinta forma, en distinto lugar o en distinto momento.

2.5 Nicho fundamental y nicho realizado

Todas las condiciones y recursos que una especie podría usar forman su nicho fundamental. La competencia y los depredadores casi siempre le impiden usarlo completo. La parte que realmente usa es su nicho realizado. Por ejemplo, una especie de percebe puede sobrevivir en toda una costa rocosa, pero un competidor más fuerte la desplaza de las rocas bajas, así que solo vive en las rocas altas.

VOCABULARIO
Nicho fundamental — todas las condiciones y recursos que una especie podría usar.
Nicho realizado — la parte del nicho fundamental que una especie realmente usa debido a la competencia y otras interacciones.
COMPRUEBA LO APRENDIDO
La trucha de arroyo y la trucha marrón compiten por los mismos insectos en un arroyo. La trucha marrón tolera agua más caliente que la trucha de arroyo. Predice qué especie tiene más probabilidad de quedarse si el arroyo se calienta poco a poco. Explica usando el término rango de tolerancia.

PARTE 2

Interacciones y poblaciones

Competencia · Depredación · Simbiosis · Crecimiento de la población · Capacidad de carga

Lección 3 · Interacciones ecológicas · Lección 4 · Crecimiento de la población y capacidad de carga

LECCIÓN 3: INTERACCIONES ECOLÓGICAS

Ningún organismo vive solo. Cada población de una comunidad interactúa con otras: compite por recursos, come o es comida, o vive en estrecha relación con otra especie. Estas interacciones determinan el tamaño de cada población.

3.1 La competencia

La competencia ocurre cuando varios organismos necesitan el mismo recurso limitado, como alimento, agua, luz, espacio o pareja. La competencia perjudica a ambos competidores, porque cada uno obtiene menos del recurso.

  • La competencia intraespecífica ocurre entre miembros de la misma especie, como dos venados machos que compiten por una pareja.
  • La competencia interespecífica ocurre entre especies distintas, como las plántulas de arce y de roble que compiten por la luz solar en el suelo del bosque.
VOCABULARIO
Competencia — una interacción en la que varios organismos necesitan el mismo recurso limitado.
Competencia intraespecífica — la competencia entre miembros de la misma especie.
Competencia interespecífica — la competencia entre miembros de especies distintas.

3.2 La depredación y la herbivoría

En la depredación, un organismo (el depredador) mata y se come a otro (la presa). Un gavilán colirrojo que atrapa un ratón de campo es un ejemplo de depredación. En la herbivoría, un animal come plantas o partes de plantas, como cuando los venados ramonean árboles jóvenes.

Las especies presa tienen adaptaciones que las ayudan a evitar a los depredadores, como el camuflaje, los colores de advertencia, la velocidad, las espinas o las sustancias tóxicas. Los depredadores tienen adaptaciones para atrapar presas, como una vista aguda, velocidad y garras.

Las poblaciones de depredadores y presas suelen subir y bajar en ciclos relacionados. Los registros del comercio de pieles de Canadá muestran que cuando abundan las liebres americanas, los linces tienen más alimento y su número aumenta. Más linces comen más liebres, así que la población de liebres baja. Con menos alimento, la población de linces también baja, y el ciclo se repite.

VOCABULARIO
Depredación — una interacción en la que un organismo mata y se come a otro.
Herbivoría — una interacción en la que un animal come plantas o partes de plantas.
COMPRUEBA LO APRENDIDO
Observa la gráfica. ¿Por qué cada pico de la población de linces llega unos años después de un pico de la población de liebres?

3.3 La simbiosis

La simbiosis es una relación estrecha y duradera entre dos especies distintas. Hay tres tipos principales:

TipoEspecie 1Especie 2Ejemplo
Mutualismo+ se beneficia+ se beneficiaLas abejas obtienen néctar de las flores; las flores son polinizadas.
Comensalismo+ se beneficia0 no se ve afectadaLos percebes viajan sobre una ballena y filtran alimento; la ballena no se ve afectada.
Parasitismo+ se beneficia (parásito)− se perjudica (huésped)Una garrapata se alimenta de la sangre de un venado cola blanca.
VOCABULARIO
Simbiosis — una relación estrecha y duradera entre dos especies distintas.
Mutualismo — una relación en la que ambas especies se benefician.
Comensalismo — una relación en la que una especie se beneficia y la otra no se ve afectada.
Parasitismo — una relación en la que una especie (el parásito) se beneficia y la otra (el huésped) se perjudica.

3.4 Especies clave y cascadas tróficas

Una especie clave tiene un efecto en su ecosistema mucho mayor de lo que sugiere su número. Si se elimina, puede cambiar toda la comunidad.

El lobo gris es un ejemplo famoso. Los lobos fueron eliminados del Parque Nacional Yellowstone hacia la década de 1920. Sin depredadores, los alces (wapitíes) se volvieron muy numerosos y se comieron los sauces y álamos jóvenes junto a los arroyos. Después de que se reintrodujeron los lobos en 1995, el número de alces bajó y los alces se movían más. Los sauces y álamos empezaron a recuperarse, lo que dio a los castores más alimento y material para sus presas, y a las aves cantoras más lugares para anidar. Una cadena de efectos como esta, que pasa por los niveles de alimentación de una red alimentaria, se llama cascada trófica.

En Pensilvania, el castor es una especie clave de otro tipo. Al construir presas, los castores convierten los arroyos en estanques y humedales que dan hábitat a ranas, patos, peces e insectos.

VOCABULARIO
Especie clave — una especie que tiene un efecto en su ecosistema mucho mayor de lo que sugiere su número.
Cascada trófica — una cadena de efectos que pasa por varios niveles de alimentación de una red alimentaria cuando cambia una población.

LECCIÓN 4: CRECIMIENTO DE LA POBLACIÓN Y CAPACIDAD DE CARGA

¿Por qué los venados, los ratones o los dientes de león no cubren toda la Tierra? Toda población puede crecer muy rápido, pero los recursos limitados y otros factores la mantienen bajo control.

4.1 Cómo se describe una población

Los ecólogos describen una población por su tamaño (el número de individuos), su densidad y su distribución (cómo están repartidos los individuos). La densidad de población es el número de individuos por unidad de área.

Densidad de población = número de individuos ÷ área

Como casi nunca es posible contar todos los individuos, los ecólogos hacen estimaciones. Pueden contar los organismos en unos cuantos cuadrados de muestra llamados cuadrantes y multiplicar, o capturar, marcar y liberar animales y luego ver cuántos animales marcados se vuelven a capturar (captura y recaptura).

VOCABULARIO
Densidad de población — el número de individuos de una especie por unidad de área.
COMPRUEBA LO APRENDIDO
Los biólogos de vida silvestre calculan que en un terreno de caza estatal de 12 km² viven 240 venados cola blanca. ¿Cuál es la densidad de población? Muestra tu trabajo.

4.2 Qué cambia el tamaño de una población

Cuatro procesos cambian el tamaño de una población. Los nacimientos y la inmigración (individuos que llegan) agregan individuos. Las muertes y la emigración (individuos que se van) quitan individuos.

Cambio en la población = (nacimientos + inmigración) − (muertes + emigración)

Si se agregan más individuos de los que se quitan, la población crece. Si se quitan más de los que se agregan, la población disminuye.

VOCABULARIO
Tasa de natalidad — el número de nacimientos en una población durante un período de tiempo.
Tasa de mortalidad — el número de muertes en una población durante un período de tiempo.
Inmigración — la llegada de individuos a una población.
Emigración — la salida de individuos de una población.

4.3 El crecimiento exponencial

Cuando los recursos son ilimitados y nada limita la reproducción, una población muestra crecimiento exponencial. La población aumenta cada generación en un número mayor, porque cada vez hay más individuos que se reproducen. En una gráfica, el crecimiento exponencial forma una curva en forma de J.

Generación0123456
Bacterias (se duplican en cada generación)1248163264

En la naturaleza, el crecimiento exponencial solo dura períodos cortos, por ejemplo cuando una especie llega a un área nueva con mucho alimento y sin depredadores, o cuando se colocan bacterias en un caldo nutritivo nuevo.

4.4 El crecimiento logístico y la capacidad de carga

En la mayoría de las poblaciones reales, el crecimiento se hace más lento a medida que escasean los recursos. Este patrón es el crecimiento logístico, que forma una curva en forma de S. El crecimiento empieza lento, se acelera y luego se hace más lento hasta estabilizarse. La población se estabiliza en la capacidad de carga (K), la población más grande que un medio ambiente puede sostener durante un período largo.

En la capacidad de carga, los nacimientos y las muertes están más o menos equilibrados. Una población puede superar brevemente la capacidad de carga, pero luego escasea el alimento o se propagan enfermedades, y la población vuelve a bajar.

VOCABULARIO
Crecimiento exponencial — un crecimiento de la población que se acelera con el tiempo y forma una curva en J cuando los recursos son ilimitados.
Crecimiento logístico — un crecimiento de la población que se hace más lento y se estabiliza en la capacidad de carga, formando una curva en S.
Capacidad de carga (K) — la población más grande que un medio ambiente puede sostener durante un período largo.

4.5 Los factores limitantes

Un factor limitante es cualquier cosa que controla el crecimiento de una población. Los ecólogos clasifican los factores limitantes en dos grupos:

Factores dependientes de la densidadFactores independientes de la densidad
Tienen un efecto más fuerte cuando la población está apiñadaAfectan a la población de la misma forma sin importar qué tan apiñada esté
Competencia por alimento, agua, espacioInundaciones, sequías, incendios
DepredaciónHuracanes, tornados, tormentas de hielo
Enfermedades y parásitos (se propagan más rápido entre muchos individuos)Clima inusualmente caluroso o frío
VOCABULARIO
Factor limitante — cualquier cosa que controla el crecimiento de una población.
Factor dependiente de la densidad — un factor limitante que tiene un efecto más fuerte cuando la población está más apiñada.
Factor independiente de la densidad — un factor limitante que afecta a una población de la misma forma sin importar su tamaño o densidad.

4.6 La capacidad de carga a distintas escalas

La capacidad de carga no es un número fijo. Cambia cada vez que cambian los recursos de un medio ambiente, y se puede medir a distintas escalas:

  • A pequeña escala: un solo estanque quizá solo pueda sostener unos cientos de ranas verdes, limitadas por los insectos que comen y los lugares para poner huevos.
  • A escala regional: algunos años los bosques de Pensilvania producen cosechas enormes de bellotas y otros años muy pocas. En un buen año de bellotas, la capacidad de carga para ratones, ardillas y venados sube, y sus poblaciones crecen al año siguiente. En un año malo, baja.
  • A escala mundial: los científicos debaten cuál es la capacidad de carga de la Tierra para los seres humanos, que depende de cuánto alimento, agua dulce y energía usa la gente.
COMPRUEBA LO APRENDIDO
Una población de 200 peces mojarra (bluegill) de un lago tiene en un año 50 nacimientos, 30 muertes, 5 peces que llegan y 10 peces que se van. ¿Cuál es la población al final del año? Muestra tu trabajo.
